はいはい の なつ — The Summer of Crawling

You say that you start, finish or keep doing something (～はじめる / ～だす / ～おわる / ～つづける), that something is “too…” (～すぎる) and that it is “easy / hard to…” (～やすい / ～にくい); in the summer when Mihai takes the N4 exam, Rosa Elena starts crawling and Ana gets ready to teach again.

To say that an action starts, ends or continues: verb stem (the ます form without ます) + はじめる / だす / おわる / つづける.
To say “too…” with ～すぎる (verbs, い and な adjectives; いい → よすぎる, ない → なさすぎる) and to use nouns in ～すぎ (のみすぎ, たべすぎ).
To say “easy to… / hard to…” with ～やすい / ～にくい and conjugate them like い adjectives.
To find out what the JLPT Japanese exam (N5–N1) looks like and to use exam vocabulary.

A Saturday afternoon at the end of June, in the flat in Cotroceni. Ioana has come for the Saturday practice. On Sunday, 4 July, Mihai is taking the N4 Japanese exam in Bucharest; Ioana is taking N3 on the same day. Rosa Elena (five and a half months) is lying on a blanket on the floor.
Mihai, how did the mock test go?
I started working through it last night, but I didn't finish it. I fell asleep halfway.
Because you study too much, until late, every evening. And you drink too much coffee.
But there's only one week left until the exam. And besides, kanji are hard to memorise. There are too many kanji that look alike.
I know what you mean. N3 kanji are hard for me to memorise too, and I'm struggling. But with flashcards they're easy to remember.
Listening is my weakest point. They speak too fast and it's hard to make out.
If you keep listening a little every day, it gradually gets easier to catch. I listen on the tram.
I listen during my lunch break at the hospital. But as soon as I start listening, I get sleepy right away.
(Laughing) That's because you're short of sleep. Rosa Elena woke up three times again last night.
Oh, look! She rolled over onto her tummy!
Lately she rolls over straight away. She might start crawling soon.
Once she starts crawling, the flat will get dangerous. We have to put covers on the sockets.
And besides, I'm going back to the school too, from September. The headmaster called me yesterday.
Ana, you're starting to teach again? That's great!
Yes. Only Monday and Thursday afternoons. During that time, Mihai's mother will look after Rosa Elena.
My mother says: “I raised Mihai, didn't I? Leave it to me.”
But I'm a bit worried. I've been at home for so long; will I still be able to teach well?
You'll be fine. Your explanations are always easy to understand.
Right, let's carry on with today's practice! Let's do some listening exercises together.
OK. But first, one more coffee…
No, you drink too much! Have tea today.
“nete shimatta” = I fell asleep (without meaning to)
“sore ni” = and besides, on top of that
“na no yo” = (explanation: it's because); (thinking aloud, male)
all the time, for a long time
su-gi-ru: the “g” is always hard, as in “go”, never soft as in “gem”. When it's attached to a verb, everything is said as one word, with no pause: no-mi-su-gi, ta-be-su-gi.
ya-su-i, ni-ku-i: three short, even syllables. When attached to a verb, don't pause between the stem and the ending: wa-ka-ri-ya-su-i, o-bo-e-ni-ku-i.
chō-ka-i: long “o” (cho-o). ju-ke-n-hyō: “hyō” is a single syllable with a long “o”, like “hyo” said quickly. The ん before “h” is nasal, without closing your lips.
1. Verb stem + はじめる / だす / おわる / つづける

Take the ます form of the verb and cut off ます: what's left is the STEM (よみます → よみ). Attach a second verb to it and you get “to start …ing”, “to finish …ing”, “to keep …ing”. You've already met two: さきはじめた (the cherry trees started to bloom) and たべおわった (I finished eating) in ch. 47.

The second verb conjugates normally: はじめる and つづける like -eru verbs (はじめた, つづけて), おわる like a godan verb (おわった, おわらなかった). Mihai: ゆうべ ときはじめた けど、ときおわらなかった (“I started working through it, but I didn't finish”).

～だす also means “to start”, but SUDDENLY, unexpectedly, without anyone planning it: あかちゃん が なきだした (the baby burst into tears), あめ が ふりだした (it suddenly started to rain). That's why it isn't used with “let's…”: ✓ たべはじめましょう, ✗ たべだしましょう.

～おわる goes mostly with actions someone does on purpose and that have a clear end (よみおわる, かきおわる, たべおわる). For things in nature you say it differently: the rain stopped = あめ が やんだ (not ふりおわった). In very polite writing you'll also see ～おえる: よみおえる.
You can also say it with a noun: べんきょう を はじめる / べんきょう を つづける. Both are correct; the stem version (べんきょう しつづける) stresses the action going on without a break.
すぎる (to go past) attached to a word means “beyond measure, too”. It's easy to form:
to eat / drink / study too much
すぎる conjugates like an -eru verb: すぎた, すぎて, すぎない, すぎます. With the ～て form you also show the consequence: はやすぎて、ききとりにくい (“it's too fast, so it's hard to make out”), あつすぎて、ねられない.
Stem + すぎ becomes a noun: のみすぎ (drinking too much), たべすぎ, はたらきすぎ, べんきょう しすぎ. It's the favourite form for short telling-offs: Ana — 「コーヒー も のみすぎ!」
Trap: いいすぎる does NOT mean “too good” but “to say too much, to go too far with words” (いう → いい + すぎる). “Too good” = よすぎる. Likewise, “too little time” = なさすぎる, not ないすぎる.
Verb stem + やすい = “easy to…”; + にくい = “hard to…”. The result is an い adjective and conjugates exactly like one: わかりやすい → わかりやすくて, わかりやすかった, わかりやすく なる; おぼえにくい → おぼえにくくて, おぼえにくくない.
Your explanations are always easy to understand.
The flashcards fit in your pocket, so they're easy to use.
If you listen every day, it gets easier to catch.
～やすい also has a second meaning: “that … easily, prone to…”: わすれやすい (forgetful / easily forgotten), かぜ を ひきやすい (who catches colds easily), やぶれやすい かみ (paper that tears easily).

Besides ～にくい there is also ～づらい: “hard to…” because it HURTS or embarrasses you personally (いいづらい = hard to say, I feel awkward). ～にくい rather describes the thing itself (かきにくい ペン = a pen that's hard to write with).
4. Review: everything that attaches to the stem
The verb stem (the ます form without ます) is a “key” you've used many times. Here they all are together, with よむ (stem よみ):
I finish reading / I keep reading
They can also be combined: はやすぎて ききとりにくい (too fast, so hard to catch), よみはじめたら、おもしろくて よみつづけた (I started reading and, since it was interesting, I kept going).
5. Culture: the JLPT exam (日本語能力試験)

にほんご のうりょくしけん (Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, JLPT) is the best-known Japanese exam for foreigners. It has five levels: from N5 (the easiest) to N1 (the hardest). It is held in July and December, in Japan and in many other countries.
reading kanji, choosing the right word
ぶんぽう・どっかい (grammar, reading)

N4 scoring: out of 180 points you need at least 90, plus a minimum in each part (38 out of 120 for vocabulary-grammar-reading, 19 out of 60 for listening). Answers are marked on a sheet in PENCIL (えんぴつ), so bring an eraser too (けしゴム). At the entrance you show your admission voucher (じゅけんひょう) and an ID.

Results of the July exam can be seen online towards the end of August; the certificate comes later, by post. N4 means, roughly, about 300 kanji and 1,500 words — exactly what you're learning in this course.

When June came, it suddenly started to get hot in Bucharest.
Mihai's summer was the summer of the Japanese exam. On the first Sunday of July he was going to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, level N4, in Bucharest.
After Rosa Elena falls asleep, Mihai opens his workbook at the kitchen table.
At first he fell asleep as soon as he opened the page. But now he keeps going for an hour every evening.
During his lunch break at the hospital he kept listening to listening exercises on his earphones.
“They speak too fast. I can hardly catch what they say,” Mihai often sighed.
Kanji were hard too. There were too many that looked alike, and he just couldn't remember them.
The flashcards Ioana had recommended fit in his pocket, so they're easy to use. Mihai kept flipping through them even while waiting for the tram.
One night, when Ana came into the kitchen, Mihai was asleep on his workbook. On the table stood no fewer than three coffee cups in a row.
“You study too much. And you drink too much coffee,” Ana said softly, and put a blanket over his shoulders.
At five months, Rosa Elena learnt to roll over onto her tummy. However often they laid her on her back, she'd immediately roll, plop, onto her tummy.
Elena boasted: “Mihai rolled over early too.”
At the end of June, Grandpa called from the village.
“Rosa Elena's little chair is almost ready. When August comes, come and get it, and bring me my great-granddaughter.”
On the other end of the line, Grandpa said, clearly pleased: “Cherry wood is hard, difficult to carve. That's exactly why it makes a good chair.”
4 July, Sunday. The morning of the exam was very hot.
The exam was held at the University of Bucharest. Ioana was taking N3 on the same day too.
Before leaving, Mihai checked his bag countless times. Admission voucher, passport, pencils, eraser.
“Five pencils? That's a bit too many, isn't it?” Ana laughed.
He was just putting his shoes on at the door when Rosa Elena burst into tears. Mihai wanted to go back, but Ana pushed him by the back: “It's fine, go!”
Ana took Rosa Elena's little hand and waved it: “Good luck, Daddy!”
In front of the university he met Ioana. “It was hot and I was nervous, so I found it hard to fall asleep last night.”
“Me, on the contrary, I fall asleep anywhere straight away. Even on my workbook.” They both laughed, and their nerves eased a little.
When the exam began, Mihai started solving the questions with all his might.
The time flew by in the blink of an eye.
In the kanji questions there were lots he had seen on his flashcards. In grammar, “~hazu” and “~tokoro” came up too.
The listening, as he'd expected, seemed too fast. But in one question a baby could be heard crying, and Mihai smiled in spite of himself.
When he finished listening to the last question, his shirt was soaked with sweat.
When he came out, Ioana was waiting for him. “How was it?” “I don't know. But I kept on solving to the very end without giving up.”
The results can be seen online at the end of August.
“And what will you do until then?” “Keep studying. I've already bought the N3 book.” Ioana laughed, amazed.
When he got home, Ana and Rosa Elena were waiting for him at the door.
“Welcome home. How was it?” “The listening was too fast… But the question with the baby crying — I'm sure I got that one right.”
Ana burst out laughing: “Well, you practise that every night.”
In August it was over 35 degrees in Bucharest every day.
Mrs Doina from next door brought them cold compote and said to Mihai: “Studying on such a scorching day? You're overdoing it!”
Rosa Elena turned seven months old. She sits up on her own and plays with Sakura's little drum.
One Sunday morning, the little drum rolled away and ended up a bit further off.
Rosa Elena reached out her hand, but she couldn't reach it. She cried a little and reached out again.
And then, propping herself up on her hands and knees, she started to move forward. Slowly, but she was definitely moving forward.
Mihai flung down his pen and came running.
Rosa Elena grabbed the little drum, turned round towards them and smiled proudly.
Mihai picked Rosa Elena up and kissed her little cheeks again and again.
When Ana sent the video to Hiroshima, Sakura replied straight away: “Hana-chan, amazing! She made it all the way to my drum!”
From then on, Rosa Elena crawled every day. She got faster and faster: the moment you took your eyes off her, she was already in another room.
One day she crawled all the way to the front door. From outside came the barking of Mr Petre's dog. Rosa Elena, facing the door, was answering: “Aaah, aaah!”
Elena boasted again: “Mihai started crawling at seven months too.”
She pulls books off the bookshelf and chews slippers. Mihai's workbook got a corner chewed off too.
“This book has thin pages, it tears easily…” said Mihai, with a face as if he were about to cry.
They put covers on all the sockets in the flat and fitted the drawers with stoppers to make them hard to open.
“There are too many dangerous things for a baby in this flat.”
Ana too started preparing her September classes.
The new textbook she got from the headmaster has lots of pictures and looks easy to use.
A message came from Cristina too: “Ana-sensei, I can't wait to have lessons with you again from September. Andrei is waiting for you too.”
In the evening, after Rosa Elena falls asleep, Mihai studies Japanese at one end of the table, and Ana prepares her classes at the other.
It was settled that on Monday and Thursday afternoons Elena would look after Rosa Elena.
“What if she cries the whole time? What will I do?” When Ana worried, Elena thumped her chest: “Who do you think raised Mihai?”
One evening at the end of August, Ana wrote in her Japanese diary:
“Rosa Elena has started crawling. Mihai keeps studying. And from September I'm starting to teach again. We're all moving forward, little by little.”
When she finished writing and turned round, Rosa Elena was moving her arms and legs in her cot, fast asleep.
“Even in her dreams she keeps on crawling.”
Ana tucked her in again with the thin summer blanket and turned off the light.
